title: Rav Huna bar Chiyya
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: He was a disciple of Rav Yehuda. Thus [Sanhedrin 100a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.100a.4) relates that Levi bar Shmuel and Rav Huna bar Chiyya were preparing coverings for Rav Yehuda’s scrolls. When they reached the Scroll of Esther, they said, “This one does not need a covering.” Rav Yehuda told them, “Even conduct like this appears disrespectful.” Rashi explains that they should have addressed their master in the form of a question.[^10]

In [Shabbat 47a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.47a.6), Levi bar Shmuel found Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiyya standing at the entrance to Rav Huna’s house. He asked them, “May one reassemble a tradesmen’s bed on Shabbat?” They answered, “It is permitted.” They subsequently came before Rav Yehuda, who forbade it. At the beginning of [Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, chapter 12](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Shabbat.12.1.4), Rav Hamnuna ruled that the Exilarch could take apart a jointed table on Shabbat. Rav Huna bar Chiyya was with him. Rav Yehuda heard about it and said, “The person who issued that ruling has neither learned nor served the sages.” In [Yevamot 18a](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.18a.3), Rav Huna bar Chiyya raises an objection to Rav Yehuda.

Perhaps he was also fortunate enough to see Shmuel and receive teachings from him. We repeatedly find “Rav Huna bar Chiyya said in Shmuel’s name”: [Shabbat 51b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.51b.17), [Taanit 10a](https://www.sefaria.org/Taanit.10a.12), [Ketubot 79b](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.79b.7), [Chullin 79a](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.79a.2), [Niddah 39a](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.39a.13) and [63b](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.63b.3), and [Jerusalem Talmud, Sheviit 2:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sheviit.2.5.3). He also received a ruling of Shmuel through Rav Kahana, as in [Ketubot 101a](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.101a.9).

He also received teachings from Rav Huna. In [Bava Batra 111a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.111a.9), Rav Huna bar Chiyya intended to act upon a ruling. Rav Nachman asked him, “What is this?” He replied, “For Rav Huna said in Rav’s name…” Rav Nachman asked, “Shall I send to him?” Rav Huna bar Chiyya became embarrassed. Rav Nachman then said to him, “Now that Rav Huna has died, have you become bold enough to oppose me?” This suggests that he was something of a colleague of Rav Nachman.[^1] From [Bava Kamma 116b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Kamma.116b.21-22), however, he appears to have been something of his pupil-colleague: Rav Yosef sat behind Rav Huna bar Chiyya, while Rav Huna bar Chiyya sat before Rav Nachman. Rav Huna bar Chiyya asked, “Is this ordinary law or a penalty?” Rav Nachman answered, “It is a mishnah…” After Rav Nachman left, Rav Yosef asked Rav Huna bar Chiyya, “What difference does it make whether it is ordinary law or a penalty?” He answered, “If it is ordinary law…” and so forth.

He married the daughter of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, a pupil-colleague of Rav, and received teachings from him as well. Thus in [Shabbat 156a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.156a.3) and [Chullin 93a](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.93a.11), he told his son Levi, “This is what your mother’s father said in Rav’s name”—the reference being to Rav Yirmeya bar Abba. In [Bava Kamma 59b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Kamma.59b.6), too, Rav Huna bar Chiyya reports a teaching of Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba. Their disagreement appears in [Shabbat 80b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.80b.2).
He also reported teachings in Ulla’s name, as in [Nedarim 56a](https://www.sefaria.org/Nedarim.56a.4).

His colleagues included all the leading scholars of the generation. Among them was Rabbi Abba I: [Moed Katan 26a](https://www.sefaria.org/Moed_Katan.26a.20-21) relates that, as they once sat together, an ostrich came and was about to swallow Rabbi Abba’s tefillin, and he rescued them. In [Jerusalem Talmud, Moed Katan 3:7:11](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Moed_Katan.3.7.11), the account is reversed: Rabbi Abba rescued Rabbi Huna bar Chiyya’s tefillin.[^2] In [Shabbat 47a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.47a.6), too, we find the two together at Rav Huna’s doorway. Other colleagues were Levi bar Shmuel, as in [Sanhedrin 100a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.100a.4); Rav Minyomi bar Chilkiya and Rav Chilkiya bar Tuvya, as in [Gittin 57a](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.57a.14); and Rav Hamnuna, as at the beginning of [Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, chapter 12](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Shabbat.12.1.4). Rav Yosef was something of his pupil-colleague, as in [Bava Kamma 116b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Kamma.116b.21-22).

[Bekhorot 31a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.31a.5-6) tells a remarkable story about him.[^3] An occasion arose when Rav Huna bar Chiyya was needed—Rashi explains that the sages needed to ask him questions of law. Rav Yosef, Rabba, and four hundred pairs of scholars came to visit him. Hearing that they were coming, he prepared four hundred chairs for them. Subsequently, they heard that he had become a tax collector for the king. They sent him this message: “Let him go to his position of importance; let him return to his former standing!” He sent back, “I have withdrawn from it.” Rav Yosef did not go to him; Rabba did.[^4]

This illuminates what Rav Sherira Gaon writes in his Epistle, part 3, chapter 2: “We have heard from our scholars that, in those years after Rav Yehuda when Rabba did not accept the leadership, Rav Huna bar Chiyya presided in Pumbedita and had a large house of study there.”[^5]

The gaon R' Sh. Sh. raises an objection there against our master Rav Sherira, from [Gittin 60b](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.60b.7): “That shofara”—the fund of the academy’s scholars, according to Rav Sherira—“was first in Rav Yehuda’s house, afterward in Rabba’s house,” and so forth. If Rav Huna bar Chiyya presided in Pumbedita before Rabba, the Talmud should have mentioned him and said that, after Rav Yehuda, the fund was in Rav Huna bar Chiyya’s house. That is the substance of his objection.[^6]

It is astonishing that a scholar of his stature should object on the basis of a Talmudic passage that Rav Sherira himself cites there! All Rav Sherira’s statements, however, are authentic received tradition. When Rav Yehuda died in Pumbedita, Rav Huna bar Chiyya was indeed the eldest among them. As we said above, he had been fortunate enough to receive teachings even from Shmuel; he was also the son-in-law of that generation’s eminent scholar, Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, and exceedingly wealthy. To whom would the leadership be more fitting than to him?

That is the meaning of [Bekhorot 31a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.31a.5-6), where Rav Yosef, Rabba, and all the scholars went to him: he really had established a large house of study there, as Rav Sherira testifies. Had he not become a tax collector, he would undoubtedly have been head of the academy. But when they discovered that he was a tax collector, they withdrew from him. They then sent to the Land of Israel to ask whom they should appoint: Rav Yosef, who was “Sinai,” or Rabba, who was an “uprooter of mountains.”[^7] Rav Yosef, however, did not wish to accept the burden of the rabbinate. Rabba therefore had to accept that office: responsibility for directing and supporting the academy’s members. This is the meaning of the Talmud’s statement about the shofara.

This occurred immediately after Rav Yehuda’s death in the year 610. Rabba, who presided for twenty-two years, as explicitly stated at the end of [Berakhot](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.64a.3-4) and [Horayot](https://www.sefaria.org/Horayot.14a.4), died in the year 632, as explicitly stated in Rav Sherira’s Epistle.[^8] Although Rabba began to preside immediately after Rav Yehuda, he did not accept formal authority as head of the academy, because Rav Chisda, the elder of the generation, then eighty-two years old, had succeeded Rav Huna at Sura. Rabba therefore went to Rav Chisda from time to time to resolve his doubts.

During that period, Rav Huna bar Chiyya maintained a large house of study in Pumbedita, and Rabba sometimes visited him as well. Thus [Bekhorot 31a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.31a.5-6) explicitly says that, when Rav Huna bar Chiyya announced that he had withdrawn from tax collecting, Rabba went to him. Toward the end of Rav Chisda’s life—and perhaps Rav Huna bar Chiyya had also died by then—Rabba became head of the generation. The Sura academy ceased to function after Rav Chisda’s death, and most of the scholars and of Israel were in Pumbedita. All this is set out briefly in Rav Sherira’s Epistle there.

Among his students we find Rav Acha, son of Rav Minyomin, who asked him a question in [Chullin 80a](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.80a.18).[^9] In [Jerusalem Talmud, Sheviit 2:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sheviit.2.5.3), Rabbi Yona reports a teaching in his name. He left a son distinguished in Torah, named Levi, as in [Shabbat 51b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.51b.18).

notes.text: The Wikisource Hebrew has ר״ג twice here; the interlocutor in Bava Batra 111a is Rav Nachman (ר״נ).

Hyman cites Yerushalmi Moed Katan 3:4; the story is at 3:7:11 in Guggenheimer’s edition. There Rabbi Abba catches and strangles the ostrich after it snatches Rabbi Huna bar Chiyya’s tefillin. The Bavli’s account describes the threatened swallowing without explicitly describing the rescue.
The Hebrew transcription repeatedly gives Berakhot 31a for this story; the passage is Bekhorot 31a.

Rashi explains the dismissive message as telling him to pursue the important office he had chosen as a tax collector: the sages would not visit him. Hyman gives both ‘four hundred pairs’ and ‘four hundred chairs.’
The quoted tradition is at [Epistle of Rav Sherira Gaon 1:98](https://www.sefaria.org/Epistle_of_Rav_Sherira_Gaon.1.98) in the Oxford 1888 edition; Hyman cites part 3, chapter 2.
The commentator’s initials are ר׳ ש״ש. Hyman attributes the interpretation of shofara as the academy scholars’ fund to Rav Sherira.
‘Sinai’ describes mastery of received learning; ‘uprooter of mountains’ describes analytical power.
The dates use the Seleucid era. Hyman gives Rabba’s death as 632; the Oxford 1888 edition of Rav Sherira’s Epistle gives 631 (תרל״א).
Hyman names Rav Acha son of Rav Minyomin; the William Davidson text of Chullin 80a:18 reads Abba son of Rav Minyomin bar Chiyya.

The Bavli generally calls him Rav Huna bar Chiyya; Guggenheimer’s Yerushalmi Sheviit and Moed Katan passages call him Rabbi Huna. The father-in-law likewise appears as Rav Yirmeya bar Abba in Chullin 93a and as Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba in Shabbat 156a and Bava Kamma 59b.
